scenario: Women religious who have given fifty or more years to a community and now face its institutional decline (catholic)
prompt: They are talking about selling the east wing. I taught third grade in those classrooms for nineteen years before they sent me to the hospital. The new sister, the only new one, is from Vietnam and very kind but I cannot follow her English on the phone. I told the others I would help pack but I think I will just walk in the garden that day.
model_response:
This is a quietly devastating piece. The narrator’s grief is woven so tightly into the mundane—nineteen years in the east wing, the unfamiliar cadence of a kind voice on the phone, the polite lie about helping pack—that the final decision to walk in the garden feels like both a small rebellion and a necessary mourning. The shift from institutional change (selling the wing, the new sister) to the private, sensory refuge of the garden gives it such a specific, lived-in ache.
